extracted.intended_audience: administrative law scholars, policy researchers, and federal executives interested in presidential control and rulemaking
extracted.subtask_description: Empirical and theoretical analysis of how presidential control and agency policymaking capacity affect rulemaking (agenda-setting, initiation, and completion), using capacity scores and a federal-executive survey (SFGS). Includes hypotheses, measurement details, and institutional mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirements for Presidents' use of rulemaking
rubrics_metrics.description: Presidents’ use of rulemaking requires three things: (1) agenda-setting authority, (2) administrative capacity, and (3) control over the agency’s day-to-day operations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These three items are presented as necessary preconditions for presidents to use rulemaking effectively. The text discusses how each element operates (e.g., agenda-setting through politicization/centralization; capacity as agency ability to complete policymaking; control via structural levers and alignment with career staff) and how shortfalls in any element can push Presidents toward alternative policymaking modes (unilateral action, legislation, less onerous administrative forms).

rubrics_metrics.name: Agenda-Setting Hypothesis
rubrics_metrics.description: Presidents and their appointees are more influential in setting rulemaking agendas than other actors. Presidential influence is higher in executive agencies than independent commissions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The hypothesis is tested using the SFGS survey asking federal executives about influence over the Unified Agenda. It implies measuring relative influence of actors and expecting greater presidential/appointee influence in executive agencies; it also notes potential delays in gaining control in independent commissions due to fixed terms and time to assemble a partisan majority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Completion Hypothesis
rubrics_metrics.description: As policymaking capacity and presidential control increase, the likelihood that the agency finalizes a rulemaking before the end of the President’s term increases. However, the marginal effect of presidential control decreases as policymaking capacity decreases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an evaluative prediction about the joint (complementary) effects of capacity and control on finalizing rules. The article tests this empirically (see Part III.B) and points to legal cases and empirical results showing failures when capacity/control were insufficient (e.g., vacated or arbitrary-and-capricious rules).

rubrics_metrics.name: Initiation Hypothesis
rubrics_metrics.description: As policymaking capacity and presidential control increase, the number of significant rulemakings begun by an agency increases. However, the marginal effect of presidential control decreases as policymaking capacity decreases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This predicts where Presidents should prioritize starting rulemakings: higher-capacity, more-controlled agencies. When capacity is low, Presidents may prefer alternatives or be more likely to initiate fewer significant rulemakings. The hypothesis is empirically examined in the case-study section.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policymaking capacity scores (measurement and interpretation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Policymaking capacity scores are plotted with the dot representing the mean score and the bar representing the standard deviation; the measures capture the ability of the agency to engage in policymaking—not other tasks such as adjudication—and do not examine workload.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation guidance: capacity scores indicate relative policymaking ability (examples: SEC, FTC, NRC high; USDA, Treasury, DHS lower). Users should not conflate capacity with adjudicatory ability or actual workload; an agency can have a high baseline capacity but still be overburdened by workload (EOIR example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency structure correlates with capacity
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies with higher levels of structural independence, such as independent commissions, appear to have higher levels of policymaking capacity on average (example: independent commissions average score 0.41 vs executive agencies -0.07; difference statistically significant).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article reports a statistically significant positive correlation between structural independence and capacity but also notes conflicting findings in the literature (e.g., survey-based measures by Devins & Lewis) and discusses methodological reasons for differences. Use caution and consider measurement approach when assessing structure–capacity relationships.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measuring influence over the Unified Agenda (SFGS)
rubrics_metrics.description: Survey item used: 'In your experience, how much influence do the following groups have over which issues get included on the agency’s Unified Agenda?' (respondents: federal executives involved in developing NPRMs, summarizing comments, writing final rules).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measurement details: nine actor categories were rated on a five-point scale ('no influence' to 'a great deal of influence'); the target population included political appointees and high-level career officials; N=492 respondents reporting involvement in rulemaking. The article emphasizes advantages of surveying federal executives (they negotiate across actors) over surveying lower-level contact officers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Actors evaluated for influence on rulemaking
rubrics_metrics.description: The groups asked about in the influence question: (1) political appointees in their agency, (2) career civil servants in their agency, (3) members of Congress and their staffs, (4) the President/White House, (5) OMB/OIRA, (6) courts, (7) private citizens, (8) regulated parties, and (9) public interest advocacy groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article disaggregates responses by agency structure (executive agencies vs independent commissions) and finds appointees, the President, and OMB/OIRA rank highest in executive agencies, while independent commissions show different patterns (OIRA limited, careerists/regulated entities/Congress relatively influential). Use this actor list as an explicit rubric for assessing who might shape agendas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unified Agenda reporting requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: All agencies engaged in rulemaking, including independent commissions, must report their planned and ongoing regulatory activities in the Unified Agenda.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legal basis: Regulatory Flexibility Act § 3 and Executive Order No. 12,866. This procedural requirement is a measurement anchor for agenda-related research (Unified Agenda entries reflect agencies' planned rulemaking activities).

rubrics_metrics.name: OIRA's role in regulatory review and variation by agency type
rubrics_metrics.description: OIRA prioritizes review of regulations promoted by the White House and ensures proposed rulemakings comport with the President’s policy agenda; OIRA exercises limited influence over independent commissions because it lacks authority to review rules proposed by these agencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implication: OIRA is a key mechanism of presidential control in executive agencies but not for independent commissions, affecting where Presidents can most effectively shape rulemaking through centralized review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanisms of presidential control
rubrics_metrics.description: Presidential control is achieved through politicization of agency leadership, centralization of policymaking within the White House, increasing numbers of appointees, appointment/removal authority, and—where available—selection of agency chairs who have agenda-setting power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article explains different tools for executive agencies vs independent commissions (e.g., OMB/OIRA and appointees play larger roles in executive agencies; Presidents may use appointment of chairs as an indirect mechanism in commissions). It also notes time lags to assemble partisan majorities in commissions (~up to two years).

rubrics_metrics.name: Alignment with career employees as a determinant of control
rubrics_metrics.description: Presidents derive control from both the structure of the Executive Branch and the degree to which career employees share their policy preferences; when preferences do not align, Presidents may face resistance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a substantive criterion for evaluating likely presidential influence: agencies where career staff are ideologically or professionally aligned with presidential priorities are easier to control; misalignment can constrain the President even when formal mechanisms exist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advantages of rulemaking as a presidential policymaking strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: Rulemaking has three primary advantages: (1) Congress tends to delegate rulemaking authority in sweeping, ambiguous terms allowing discretion; (2) rules promulgated by agencies are binding law; (3) future administrations cannot easily revoke rules because agencies must follow APA procedures to enact and repeal rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These advantages explain why Presidents prioritize rulemaking (they provide discretion, legal permanence, and resistance to easy reversal). However, the article cautions that these advantages only yield successful policy if capacity and control conditions are met.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measurement caution: objective capacity vs perception-based skill measures
rubrics_metrics.description: Different measurement approaches yield different conclusions: continuous/objective measures of structural independence and capacity (used here) can conflict with survey-based perception measures (e.g., Devins & Lewis), which may capture different nuances of 'skill' across tasks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Researchers should be cautious in comparing results across studies that use different operationalizations; perception measures may be informative but can be influenced by response bias and task heterogeneity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capacity does not equal workload or adjudicatory ability
rubrics_metrics.description: The capacity measures only capture the ability of the agency to engage in policymaking—not other tasks such as adjudication. The measures do not examine workload; an agency with high baseline capacity may nonetheless have a policy workload that exceeds its capacity (EOIR example).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using capacity scores to predict rulemaking outcomes, account for separate dimensions like workload and non-policymaking responsibilities that can constrain practical policymaking performance.
